claims.text: Quinary or higher metallic nanoparticles with equal or near-equal atomic ratios can initially exist as a single-phase solid solution.
Long-term structural and chemical stability across 473–1923 K is primarily governed by atomic-diffusion kinetics.
Changing or removing capping ligands modulates the rate of surface atomic diffusion.
Annealing time and temperature modulate surface and bulk atomic diffusion.
Sufficiently activated surface and bulk diffusion drives local segregation followed by phase separation.
Low diffusion barriers at elevated temperature allow atoms to overcome configurational-entropy stabilization of the solid solution.
Increased atomic mobility produces nanoscale compositional fluctuations and secondary-phase domains.
Enhanced surface passivation slows diffusion and thereby preserves a homogeneous single-phase structure.
Robustly ligand-capped nanoparticles will retain greater chemical homogeneity and single-phase character than minimally capped or uncapped nanoparticles under identical thermal exposure.
Extended thermal exposure promotes phase separation and chemical inhomogeneity.
Alloy composition and annealing temperature influence phase stability and the length scale of decomposition in high-entropy alloys.
The predicted surface-treatment effect should hold when composition and particle size are fixed and oxidation and substrate interactions are controlled.
TEM, XRD, and EDS mapping can be used to compare phase separation, crystallographic phases, and compositional uniformity between capped and uncapped samples.
Similar phase separation in capped and uncapped samples under identical thermal conditions would falsify the claim that surface-treatment-modulated diffusion governs stability.
